architecture: Two-tier upgradeability. Contracts there is exactly one of (reserve pool, factory, router, hook, yield adapter, guard) are ERC1967/UUPS proxies, upgraded one at a time. Contracts there are many of, one set per market (brand token, treasury, fee vault, buyback engine, lockbox), sit behind UpgradeableBeacons so one upgradeTo moves every market at once.
architectureCorrection: An earlier revision of the field above ended: the TimelockController owns every proxy and every beacon. THAT IS FALSE, and it was written from the deploy script's own log line without checking the chain. Verified via owner() on chain 4663: the timelock owns the guard, the reserve pool, the yield adapter and all ten beacons - but the ProtocolFeeHook, AssetMarketFactory and MarketRouter proxies are owned outright by the deployer EOA, which can upgradeToAndCall all three instantly, with no timelock and no delay. Simulated eth_call from that EOA returns 0x on all three; from any other address it reverts OwnableUnauthorizedAccount. This is CRITICAL-1 in ASSET_MARKETS_AUDIT_UPGRADEABLE.md. Two independent reasons no check caught it: DeployAssetMarkets.s.sol:462 inspects only the RESERVE POOL's owner (which genuinely is the timelock, so its warning correctly stays silent), and even pointed at the right contracts its test is owner.code.length == 0, which is false for a 7702-delegated EOA (23 bytes).

The CRITICAL is the ownership defect above and is the only finding exploitable with no market existing. marketCount() == 0 and the pool holds 0 USDG, so nothing is exposed yet - that is the window to fix it in. governance.timelockNote: 48h. It owns the guard, the reserve pool, the yield adapter and all ten beacons - but NOT the hook, factory or router proxies, which the deployer EOA owns outright and can upgrade with zero delay (see architectureCorrection and CRITICAL-1 in the audit). Where the timelock does apply it is load-bearing: it is the only thing standing between a leaked key and an instant rewrite of every brand token, vault, engine and lockbox implementation. Raising the delay later is cheap; lowering it always costs the delay then in force.
governance.timelockRoles: Verified on chain. The deployer EOA holds PROPOSER_ROLE, EXECUTOR_ROLE and CANCELLER_ROLE. It does NOT hold DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE - the timelock holds that itself (constructed with admin = address(0)), and OZ 5.7.0 dropped the separate TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE in favour of DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, which getRoleAdmin confirms administers all three. So roles are changeable, but only by the timelock acting on a proposer's schedule - and this EOA is the sole proposer, which makes it the only party able to grant itself admin and means no second party exists who could revoke it. It carries an EIP-7702 delegation (cast code returns 0xef010063c0c19a282a1b52b07dd5a65b58948a07dae32b) to an unidentified 11185-byte contract that answers VERSION() 1.3.0 but reverts every storage-reading selector. Even if that delegate enforces m-of-n on outgoing calls, the EOA key can still sign a plain transaction and revoke the delegation at will, so control reduces to one key regardless.
governance.guardianNote: The deployer EOA. The API is pause()/pauseTarget(address)/unpause()/unpauseTarget(address)/setGuardian(address) - there is no halt(), resume() or permanent-halt flag. The asymmetry is real and verified by probe: the guardian may pause instantly with no timelock, but ONLY the timelock owner may unpause, change the guardian or upgrade the guard. So it cannot trap funds - SharedReservePool._redeem deliberately carries no whenNotPaused and PooledBrandToken does not inherit GuardedUpgradeable at all, so holders can always exit 1:1. It is not limited to pausing in the sense the earlier note implied: the same EOA also owns the hook, factory and router proxies outright and is the protocol treasury. Move the guardian to a second key.

liveBeacons._warning: READ THIS BEFORE UPGRADING ANYTHING. Step 2 re-deployed all five beacons instead of reusing step 1's, so the set that is actually wired in is SPLIT across the two steps: brandToken and treasury come from step 1, vault/engine/lockbox come from step 2. Five beacons and five implementations were deployed and are referenced by nothing - see orphanedDeployments. Upgrading an orphaned beacon spends gas and changes no market while appearing to succeed. These five addresses were read back off chain via pool.brandTokenBeacon(), pool.treasuryBeacon() and factory.beacons(), not transcribed from script output.

core.protocolFeeHookNote: A MINED address: v4 reads a hook's permissions from the low 14 bits of the hook's own address, and 0x...C0CC carries 0xcc = beforeSwap | afterSwap | both return-deltas. The proxy address is permanent; upgrading the implementation does not move it, which is what keeps every existing pool valid.

parameters.tradingSkimNote: The trading skim goes to the PROTOCOL TREASURY, not to the market's BrandFeeVault. This is deliberate: the vault's only revenue is float yield. Consequence worth stating plainly - trading fees do NOT fund the buyback, only float yield does, and BuybackEngine.execute pays the skim like any other trader. Bound one-shot per pool at market creation, so it is immutable for the life of each pool while factory.protocolTreasury remains mutable via setProtocolParams.
parameters.buybackMinNotionalNote: Lowered from 100000000 ($100) to 1000000 ($1) on 2026-09-11 in tx 0x74d03798b15e7712e1969af37835d5f45d7e6db0e5a2a4ac7839fd000bd72788 (block 60502633), so the buyback can actually be exercised at current float. FUTURE MARKETS ONLY: minNotional is stamped into each BuybackEngine at initialize and has no setter, so markets 1-9 keep the $100 floor permanently. minInterval, twapWindow and maxDeviationBps were deliberately left at 21600/1800/200 - the shorter window and wider band used in the fork rehearsal would have weakened the price guard on every market users create. Rehearsed in test/markets/BuybackTestMarketFork.t.sol.

orphanedDeployments._note: Deployed and paid for, referenced by nothing. Step 1 deployed all five beacons but only brandToken and treasury are consumed (by the reserve pool); step 2 then deployed a second set of all five and the factory consumes vault/engine/lockbox from that set. Harmless on chain - each is owned by the timelock and points at a valid implementation - but they are a trap for anyone upgrading by address, and roughly ten deployments of wasted gas. Fixing it means DeployAssetMarkets.s.sol taking step 1's beacon addresses as inputs rather than calling ProtocolStack.deployBeacons a second time.

THE BUYBACK CANNOT FIRE AT CURRENT FUNDING. The deployer holds 304,847,650 base units = $304.85 USDG. test_fork_realWallet_floatIsFarTooSmallToEverBuyBack passes and measures it directly: $229.34 of float earns $10.97 of Morpho yield across four markets in a year, against a minNotional of $100 per round. Since only float yield funds the buyback now, not trading fees, roughly $2,000+ of float is needed for a single $100 round per year. Fund the wallet or lower minNotional; both are decisions, not code changes.

operationalNotes: forge HANGS on this deployment unless Sourcify is short-circuited. Step 2 blocked indefinitely at ~1% CPU, twice, in foundry_evm_traces::identifier::external::SourcifyFetcher::fetch: the trace contains PoolManager, PositionManager and Permit2, which are not in local artifacts, so forge tries to label them via sourcify.dev and that request never returns. --disable-labels does NOT stop the fetcher. What works is failing the request fast while leaving the RPC alone: HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:9 HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:9 NO_PROXY=rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com. Step 1, PreflightMainnet and VerifyAssetMarketsMainnet do not need it. Worth putting in the runbook, because it looks exactly like a chain problem and is not.

A standalone `forge script` simulation of step 2 (no --broadcast) is redundant and also hangs the same way. --broadcast simulates the whole script first, including the post-deploy wiring and venue assertions, and sends nothing if any of it fails.

script/rehearse-mainnet.sh was repaired for this architecture. It parsed broadcast/run-latest.json by contractName, but every proxy now reports as ERC1967Proxy, so its dict collapsed all of them onto whichever deployed last. It now reads the deploy scripts' own labelled output.

script/VerifyAssetMarketsMainnet.s.sol asserted feeRecipientOf(poolId) == market.feeVault, which was the previous generation's design and reverts on every market now that the skim goes to the protocol treasury. It now asserts the recipient is non-zero and prints both it and the current treasury, because registerPool binds one-shot at creation while setProtocolParams can move the treasury later - a strict equality would false-alarm on a healthy deployment.
